turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Tuesday, the tenth of November. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Three up top. Qatar's prime minister carried an Iranian proposal into the Oval Office yesterday. [pause] Forty-five minutes behind a closed door, and neither side has published a word since.
Nvidia's board has opened an investigation into its own founder — and a Singapore-registered company is standing in the middle of it.
And later, a hobby whose entire point is obeying a fourteenth-century fencing master. [deadpan] With a sword.
[curious] Obeying him how? Literally following instructions?
Line by line, out of the book he wrote. Hold that. Start in Washington.

Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani spent about forty-five minutes with President Trump around noon on Monday, carrying an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Closed to the press. No photograph has surfaced.
[thoughtful] And the strait is why this matters outside the room.
It's the only sea exit from the Gulf. In a normal year about a fifth of the oil the world burns goes through it — and since the war began it's been close to shut.
So the price does the talking.
On Monday crude fell again, hard. About five per cent, on a meeting whose contents nobody has described.
[skeptical] That's a lot of conviction about a room nobody was in.

And Washington ran two tracks in a day. Secretary of State Rubio called Iran's terms not just unacceptable, but in some cases outrageous and ridiculous. Then the other track: the president told CNN renewed strikes were highly unlikely to prove necessary — then added the military had picked out thirty-eight bridges in Iran it could destroy in, his words, literally one hour.
[exhales] That's a very specific kind of reassurance.
[wry] It's a number you say out loud on purpose.
[thoughtful] So what can you actually stand up?
The absence. Qatar's foreign ministry news index, read Tuesday morning, still ends at a seventh of November call with the Saudis. There is no readout of Washington at all.
[curious] And your sceptic goes further.

Fereidun Fesharaki of FGE NexantECA told Bloomberg Television we are even worse than we were before the June memorandum. His firm's note is blunter — a Democratic House and Senate leaves the president a two-month window to strike Iran again.
[pause] So the argument isn't that a deal is hard.

It's that the calendar rewards one more strike first. They rate a strike before the new Congress convenes as high, and see Hormuz flows recovering only gradually from March next year — four months later than Monday's rally is pricing. That's the trade the oil market made yesterday, whether it meant to or not.
There's a second table today.

Abu Dhabi. American, Ukrainian and Russian delegations — the first talks of this kind in nine months. But the agenda is security guarantees and the machinery for monitoring a ceasefire. The terms of a ceasefire are explicitly excluded.
[scoffs] So they're negotiating the referee before they negotiate the match.

That's the line in the book, word for word, and nobody's optimistic on the record. What would make it real: a published document naming a guarantor, a mechanism and a date. Three rounds this year have produced none.
Money — because the oil story lands here too.
The cheapest oil in five months stopped making money cheaper this week.
[curious] Unpack that.

Brent fell into the low nineties from above a hundred and twelve. America's ten-year inflation expectation fell eight basis points with it, to two point two two per cent. But the ten-year real yield rose, to two point six six.
So the inflation premium drains out —
— and the real cost of capital rises underneath it. Nominal yields barely move, and nothing gets easier. That's the regime in one line.
What does that mean for a portfolio?
World equities carry the adjustment, because two point six six is the highest real cost of capital this cycle has taken into a drawdown. Global bonds hedged, barely — insurance, not a position.
Any serious dissent?
Jordi Visser of twenty-two V Research says it wasn't conviction that broke, it was gross exposure. His words: they cannot get the gross down enough.
Home. Punggol.
The Land Transport Authority told ComfortDelGro on Saturday to stop testing U-turns at a Punggol Field junction — a day after telling Grab to pause junction testing in the same estate.
So what links them?
Not a fault. A moment. Each vehicle carries a trained person whose job is to take over when the machine shouldn't be trusted — and on the fifth, two hours apart, both of them did.
[thoughtful] So the takeover is the common factor, not the software.

In the first one a Grab shuttle was turning left as a schoolgirl crossed. The recorded data shows it had detected her and was tracking her; it braked and steered right. Then the operator took control. Nobody was touched.
Did anyone go and ask residents?

Twelve, at the Punggol Coast Mall pick-up point. Tan Kar Yeow, forty-six, says parents crossing with small kids now have to watch for driverless vehicles too. Mister Lou, twenty-nine, backed the trial — somebody has to go first.
[warmly] I like Mister Lou.
[wry] Mister Lou is carrying a lot of the national mood. But the sceptic is why this ran at all.
Go on.

In January a driverless vehicle clipped a road divider at Edgedale Plains. The authority found it had spotted the obstacle and moved into the next lane, and that simulation suggested it would have finished the manoeuvre safely without manual intervention.
[pause] And the human?
The officer's takeover disengaged autonomous mode, and he couldn't finish in time. The takeover caused the crash. What would settle this week's version: the same simulation, published.
Technology. The board and the founder.
Nvidia's board announced on Sunday it's opening an independent investigation into whether its founder and chief executive, Jensen Huang, had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
[gasps] That is not a normal sentence.
Huang told staff the same day he had been unfaithful to his wife. His words: my actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.
And this is governance, not tabloid, because —
Because of who holds the inquiry. A committee of independent directors with outside counsel. The board says it has no reason to believe secrets were compromised, and Huang stays in post.
[thoughtful] A company worth four and a half trillion dollars has taken custody of its own founder.
That's the sentence, and it's the spine of the whole issue.
And the Singapore thread?

The woman named in the reporting, Alice Huang — no relation — was a senior executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-registered data-centre company. It bought roughly four point eight billion dollars of Nvidia equipment and has been under American investigation since twenty twenty-four. Neither Huang has been charged.
How did the street take it?
Down four point two seven per cent while every other big chip name rose. Five houses published within a day, and none cut its rating.
[pause] So nobody thinks it changes the business.
Nobody. Though the bull case and the bear case agree on one thing — there is no successor. Which is a reason to worry about the company, not about the chips.
Home lab — something changed hands there too.

Home Assistant, the free program that runs a smart home from a box in your own flat, released a version that swallows the unofficial shop its enthusiasts have used for years. It's now official, renamed the Marketplace.
[thoughtful] So the shop becomes the shop. How did the forum take it?
A hundred and fifty-one posts in five days. One user, within three hours: its only reason for existence is literally just to get HACS.
[laughs] Brutal. Any case for?
The best one: so that there is now a team of people supporting it instead of one person. A single-maintainer dependency inside hundreds of thousands of homes was the worse risk.
And the sceptic?
That it's the same shop with a gatekeeper attached. What would settle it: the first time the Marketplace refuses to list something, and why.
The Kit. Something got cheaper.
XREAL cut the price of its Aura glasses three weeks after setting it, and is refunding early buyers a hundred and eighty dollars or two hundred.
What's actually been measured on it?

[deadpan] Nothing. By anyone independent. A cut that fast, with refunds attached, is worth more attention than the product — and the only hands-on detail is a sponsored review, paid for by XREAL. And every Reddit path was unreachable for this whole build, so there's no owner sentiment in the book at all.
So the honest position is —
Not which configuration. Wait for somebody with a photometer.
[amused] Atelier — secateurs. I did not expect to enjoy this page.

Nobody ever does. They're one of the last tools you can genuinely buy once, and the test isn't the steel — it's the parts list. A pruner is four things that wear out: blade, counter-blade, spring, pivot. A maker either sells those four separately, or sells you a sealed object to replace.
And Felco sells them separately.
Felco sells every part of the Felco Two, including the washer. Its drawing floats every component on its own number — bushing, thumb catch, spring washer.
[laughs] You can buy the washer.
Seventy-six francs ninety, lifetime warranty. Its weakness is the counter-blade, riveted in.
And the one that cuts better?

A Yamagata forge called Tobisho, fourth generation, founded in nineteen thirty. Nine thousand nine hundred yen — one integral forging, so nothing to replace. That's the trade of the whole page, in two tools.
[curious] And the brands?

The sceptic names what nobody prints. Niwaki is a brand, not a forge — eighty to ninety pounds with no replaceable blade, against an Okatsune at forty-eight with a published hardness and blades you can buy.
[deadpan] Logo tax.
Logo tax.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every single morning with this one.
[laughs] It's a tradition, you can't stop it. What have we got?
HEMA. Historical European martial arts — the reconstruction of how Europeans actually fought, from the instruction books their own masters wrote between roughly thirteen hundred and nineteen hundred.
So this isn't Olympic fencing.

Olympic fencing descends from one narrow duelling tradition, standardised into three weapons and an electric wire. The difference is where the authority sits. A sport fencer obeys a rulebook. A HEMA fencer is trying to obey a dead man.
[pause] Say more.
The dead man, mostly, is Johannes Liechtenauer. His late-fourteenth-century verse was deliberately written to be obscure, then explained by generations of glossators.
[curious] How many people are we talking about, globally?
You'll read there are a hundred and sixty thousand practitioners in the United States. No survey behind it — it traces to an article extrapolating from Facebook advertising-audience data.
[scoffs] That's not a count of people. That's a count of interest.
And the same page's own club finder listed two hundred and fifteen American schools. We print the two hundred and fifteen.
So what do you count instead?

Fights. A global rating site counts bouts, not people who say they fence — twenty-one thousand four hundred and twenty-three fighters, four hundred and eighteen thousand six hundred and ninety-six bouts.

And Germany's federation, the best-governed body in the sport, reported four thousand one hundred and thirty-five fencers. They volunteered the comparison themselves: German Olympic fencing has over twenty-three thousand members. The honest shape of this hobby is small, not large.
Okay — gear. Because I know that's where you live.

A training sword is called a feder. Three hundred to twelve hundred euros, and almost none of that difference is the steel — the serious makers all use the same alloy at the same hardness. What you pay for is flex, balance and a hand-guard.
[curious] And flex matters because —
Because it's what tournaments measure. They bend the sword against a scale and read the force off.
[gasps] They measure your sword at the door?
They measure your sword at the door. Too stiff and it can injure; too whippy and you can't control it.
So how do you choose?
This is the most useful thing a newcomer can know: you buy flex to the ruleset of the events you intend to enter. Not to taste. A blade gets rejected for being too flexible as easily as too rigid.
And prices from the makers?

Regenyei starts at two hundred and eighty euros before tax. At the top, a Fechtschule feder from Arms and Armor is twelve hundred and fifty dollars, copied from originals in the Metropolitan Museum, in a run of ten. And the sport's loudest argument is now conducted with instruments. Sean Franklin of Sword STEM measured three hundred and eighty-one feders against genuinely sharp swords, and found the sharps weren't qualitatively different in flex.
What's the cost of walking in here?
Singapore has exactly two places to learn. Bastion, on Jalan Pemimpin, three minutes from Marymount, founded in twenty seventeen by a married couple who picked the sport up in Britain.
Walk-in price?

Twenty-one fifty for a first adult session, ninety minutes, all gear provided. Membership then runs from two hundred and two fifty a month. And they lend gear — try before you buy anything, because the equipment is most of the money.
[curious] And if you do buy?

The arithmetic turns unfriendly. Swords are controlled items here, so the import route runs through the police licensing department. Shipping one feder from Hungary is a hundred and fifty euros against forty inside Europe, plus nine per cent tax on the lot. A two-eighty euro sword lands nearer four seventy. [exhales] And then it rusts.
Right — the climate.
One maker's care page is blunt: blades should not be stored in their leather sheaths, because leather holds moisture longer than the air around us. Here that's a weekly ritual, not an annual one.
Any hard instruction for a buy-once reader?
One, from a ruleset, three words long. No Red Dragons.
[laughs] What on earth is a Red Dragon?

The cheapest and most common gloves in the hobby. The rules say purpose-built gloves with hard hand protection; lacrosse gloves are not sufficient; no Red Dragons. The budget tier doesn't lead anywhere — the events have named it and excluded it. A tournament-legal kit is roughly fifteen hundred US dollars before shipping and tax.
[thoughtful] And the sceptic isn't about money at all, is it.

No. The institutions are thinner than the sport. North America's flagship event posted a hiatus notice that still stands: there currently exist no future plans, because we don't have the answers. Europe's flagship has no event in the ratings for thirteen months, and its domain redirects to a for-sale page.
[pause] So the books survive and the organisers don't.
Seven people edited the free library in the last thirty days. Seven, against six hundred and sixty-two registered users, maintaining the whole thing.
Culture. Godzilla did something nobody's done.

Godzilla Minus Zero led the American box office and Japan on the same three days — the first Japanese live-action film to top both markets in one weekend. An estimated thirty-one point six million dollars.
[curious] You said estimated.
Two cautions, both the studio's. That figure is still marked estimated by the trade's own tracker, and the Japanese numbers are distributor-reported rather than measured independently.
How's it reviewing?
[wry] Depends which number you read. Ninety per cent of critics recommended it. The average of their actual scores is seventy-four.
[thoughtful] Both honest. Only one's a verdict.
Thirty-four positive, ten mixed, not one negative — a film almost nobody dislikes and few call great. The complaint, when there is one, is that it's a repeat.
Family desk — the one study that really lands.

Ohio. A hundred and twenty-six girls aged ten to fourteen, six months of their own cycle records. Pain in nearly three-quarters of cycles — and health, school and activities each affected in about one cycle in five.
[pause] One in five. That's a rehearsal a month.
That's the line for a parent. A child missing a rehearsal every month isn't reporting unusual pain. She's reporting ordinary pain, repeatedly.
Is there better data?

Smaller, better instruments. One group followed forty-three girls for years, collecting a mean of five hundred and eighty-nine urine samples each, to date the cycles biochemically rather than by recall.
[gasps] Five hundred and eighty-nine. Each.
Each. And the most useful sentence on this subject comes out of it: menstrual pain was not associated with physical activity, anxiety or depression.
[warmly] So worsening pain early on isn't a sign something's wrong.
It's mostly ovulation becoming established. General guidance, not medical advice.
Fitness. Two minutes.

Brad Schoenfeld's group, published Friday. Forty trained lifters, eight weeks. Those told to rest a fixed two minutes gained as much as those resting however long they liked — and finished about twenty-nine per cent sooner.
[excited] That's half an hour of my life back.

[deadpan] Precisely what it is, and precisely what it isn't. Muscle growth favoured the fixed group by a tenth of a standard deviation; performance was flat at zero. It's a stopwatch effect, not a physiological one. One caveat before you copy it: neither the abstract nor the preprint states the participants' ages. The only write-up that does puts them at eighteen to forty. Not evidence in mid-forties lifters.
Diary — one thing to actually do.

One live deadline on the page: Art SG's early bird ends on the twenty-fourth, two-for-one adult passes, under-sixteens free with a paying adult. And Christmas Wonderland finally has dates — though for the fifth issue running the ticket line still reads: prices will be released soon.
[scoffs] Classic. And the Table?

Three openings out of roughly sixty written up since mid-October. The ledger bars a hundred and thirty-one venue names that have had their two runs, so the window is fully enumerable now — and it's been eaten.
[curious] What stood up?

A patisserie opened by two friends who met playing League of Legends; a build-your-own pasta stall in a Serangoon supper hawker centre; and a kueh maker who's moved out of a dim Thomson basement into Sin Ming.
[warmly] And she still uses her grandmother's mould.
Thirty years old, wooden. And we label it honestly — that one's a relocation, not a debut.
The long read. Japan.
On the nineteenth of June, nine people in their thirties, forties and fifties met in an event bar in Nagoya to talk about how little they had been eating.
[pause] Go on.
The man who organised it is thirty-three. Eighteen months of banana for breakfast, oatmeal for lunch, soba at night. Same clothes daily. All of it to fill his annual tax-free investment allowance.
Why does that have a name?
Because enough people are doing it. NISA binbō — NISA poverty. It reached the floor of the Diet in March, and last week it was shortlisted for Japan's word of the year.
[exhales] And the scheme itself is bad?

Rather good, actually. Remodelled at the start of twenty twenty-four, exemption made permanent, ceilings raised. It has worked far better than intended — over thirty million accounts. One in four Japanese adults.
[thoughtful] So a ceiling was announced.
And a certain kind of person read it as an instruction. The minister who administers the policy has said so herself: accumulation becoming the goal was never intended at all.
Is there a number that shows the substitution?

One, published in January, before anyone had a word for it. Among Japanese in their twenties who invest, the monthly sum going into investments rose about twenty per cent in a year — while the share spending anything at all on investment in oneself, meaning skills, study and qualifications, fell from twenty-nine point six per cent to twenty-four point three.
[pause] They increased what they put into index funds by a fifth —
— and cut what they put into themselves.
Is anyone pushing back on the panic?

Seriously, and in Japanese. One economist says the surveys don't show many twenty-somethings cutting living costs to max the allowance. About eighty per cent of Japanese in their twenties have no account at all. It's a vanguard, not a generation.
[curious] But you've got something nobody in Tokyo seems to have said.
The apparatus now urging Japanese households into the stock market isn't merely similar to the one that spent seventy years urging them to save. It's the same institution.
[gasps] The same —

Same secretariat lineage, opposite instruction. The Central Council for Savings Promotion was founded in nineteen fifty-two, chaired by a former governor of the Bank of Japan, with its secretariat inside the Bank's head office. It was wound up in twenty twenty-four — the year the new allowance began — and handed to the new financial-education agency.
[drawn out] Same machine. Opposite verb.

Identical grammar: abstain now, be rewarded later. Seventy-eight years of a state telling its citizens that the virtuous thing to do with money is not to spend it. The object changed; the sentence didn't.
[thoughtful] So NISA poverty isn't a new pathology.

It's deflation-era self-denial wearing an index fund. Which is why the remedy sounds so thin — asked what to do about people over-complying, the minister offered financial education. The output of the agency that inherited the savings council.
A nudge with no brake.

And the timing is bad. The Nikkei is about nineteen per cent below its June peak. The first real drawdown of the new era is arriving at the most leveraged-by-abstinence cohort the country has produced — as a social event, because the people holding the losses skipped dinners to buy in.
Does anyone defend them?

Japan's most-followed retail voice does, and it deserves printing in full rather than sneering at. Quote: NISA poverty — absolutely fine. It's that person's life. The people criticising NISA poverty won't take responsibility for you.
[warmly] He's not wrong. The critics don't pay.
The critics don't pay. The question the next decade will put to Japan is whether the state that spent seventy-eight years teaching the sentence will.
[pause] And that's the handover.

It's been the whole book. A safety operator takes the wheel — and in January the takeover was what caused the crash. A board takes custody of its own founder. A volunteer shop absorbed by the project it served.
A grandmother's mould. A dead fencing master's verse.
A Yamagata forge that will sell you a better tool and nothing to repair it with. [pause] A handover isn't a transfer of power.
[thoughtful] It's a transfer of habits.
And the habits usually win.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
